cues.text:
Picture two issues in the same
repository. One is about zero
quantities.

Another asks for a clearer error
message. The issue ID and expected
behavior change.

The location of the test suite may stay
the same across both.

Put recurring project conventions where
the agent can load them,

and keep the individual issue details in
the prompt you send for that task.

Open a Markdown template in the training
repository.

Write a request that takes an issue and
the current source and tests as inputs.

Ask for the proposed edit, the affected
files, and a way to verify it.

The template should end at a plan you
can review.

On the approved Copilot setup, paste the
filled-in text into chat to run it.

Start Plan in the current branch and
attach the issue, validator,
and matching test file.

Paste the template with the issue
reference filled in.

The response should identify the
existing comparison and explain why a
zero test would expose it.

Open the cited lines and check them
yourself. If a file name is unfamiliar,

confirm it in the workspace before
accepting the plan.

Open the repository root in VS Code. For
this Copilot example,

find or create the project instructions
file in the dot GitHub folder.

Add the convention that unit tests use
the existing unittest suite under tests.

Keep the rule short and include a
reliable reference for the verification
command.

If instructions already exist, edit the
existing guidance with your team.

Open the agent customizations view and
find the instruction file.

Then start a fresh chat in the same
workspace. Ask for a regression plan
without repeating the test convention.

Where your client shows references,
confirm the file was included.

Read the proposed test location and
framework. File discovery and correct

use give you two different things to
check.

The prompt asks for a particular piece
of work. The instruction file supplies
reusable project conventions.

Required checks and actual tool
permissions enforce separate boundaries.

Some VS Code versions also offer
runnable prompt files,

with support depending on the selected
harness.

The Markdown template in this example is
ready to paste.

In the next lesson, we’ll make a
recurring procedure into a skill.

Use the template for a second synthetic
issue. Swap the issue reference and
attach the current files for that task.

Compare the two plans and find one part
that changed because the requirement
changed.

Then find the test convention that
carried over.

A teammate should be able to reproduce
that setup in a fresh session with the
same project files.
